Librarian here. The issues surrounding this are a bit more complex than you might expect.

The purpose of a public library is first and foremost the provision of access to information for the general public. As it is funded by the taxpayer and furnished by the government, the censorship of its materials may constitute a violation of the First Amendment.

However, space in a library is finite. Books and other items are discarded simply because they were not circulating, and room needed to be cleared for other, more popular books. As for assemblies such as this one, a great deal more space is needed. Someone at the Boston Public Library must have made a conscious decision to allow these drag queens to read to the children, on the library's time and dime.

Here are some questions I would have for my colleagues at the BPL: Why did you allow this group to come to the library, and interact with the patrons in the manner they did? If it was because they filed a request to do so, would you honor a similar request by a group whose real or implicit values did not meet with your approval? Did the book they read to the children or other teachings imparted by the group espouse claims that have not been proven (e.g., "Gender is a social construct"), or are a matter of personal opinion? What would you do if the parents of one of these children complained that the presentation was inappropriate? Would your response be the same if the presentation involved lessons with which you personally disagree?

In cases involving freedom of speech, public funding of speech, and a limited amount of time and space in which to speak, there are no easy answers.
